# Carbonylative Aminative Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling: Pd-Catalyzed Synthesis of Amides from Vinyl/Aryl Halides and Boronic Acids

**Authors:** Jianhan Zhou; Dalton Raykowski; Zuzanna Kowalski; Shangyu Li; Yifan Ping; Yongrui Luo; Eugene E. Kwan; Richard Y. Liu

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, 12 Oxford St., Cambridge, MA 02138, United States | bProcess Research and Development, Merck & Co., Inc., Rahway, NJ 07065, United States

## Abstract

Amide synthesis is critical for the development of pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and functional materials. Here, we report a four-component variant of the Pd-catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura coupling that repurposes partners conventionally used for C–C bond formation to instead yield amides. The sequential insertion of CO, from Mo(CO)6 as a convenient surrogate, and NH, from O-(diphenylphosphinyl)hydroxylamine (DPPH), allows access to a broad scope of secondary amides bearing aromatic and olefinic groups, including enamides, α,β-unsaturated amides, and α,β-unsaturated enamides. Drug-like analogs can be rapidly assembled, and we show that “reverse amide” counterparts can be generated from the same starting materials.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Cross-coupling methods,1–5 such as the Suzuki–Miyaura and Buchwald–Hartwig coupling (SMC and BHC) reactions, have become indispensable for the synthesis of complex molecules with applications as pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and advanced materials.1,3,5–7 In the exploration of chemical space for small-molecule research and development, organic synthesis still represents a rate- and creativity-limiting step.8–10 It is logical to expect that rational expansion of the cross-coupling toolbox might play an important role in addressing this bottleneck.

An ever-expanding range of electrophiles and nucleophiles has become amenable to catalytic cross-coupling.11–19 In a complementary direction, our group has been interested in methods to repurpose popular cross-coupling partners to form alternative products through modifications of the reaction mechanism. Insertive coupling, in which a small group is incorporated between the two coupling partners, is a prototypical class of altered cross-coupling reactions (Fig. 1a, Insertive coupling). Carbonylative Suzuki–Miyaura reactions, for example, have been extensively developed, enabling the incorporation of CO to access ketone products.20–22 Heteroatom insertion remains comparatively underexplored. SO2 insertion has been demonstrated as a powerful strategy for sulfone synthesis.23 More recently, strategies have emerged that enable the formal insertion of nitrogen, oxygen, and carbene equivalents between Suzuki–Miyaura coupling partners, providing access to amines, ethers, and triarylmethanes24–27 from a unified substrate pool.28

Amides are among the most prevalent functional groups in both natural and synthetic molecules, occupying a central role in biology. They are most commonly constructed through the condensation of carboxylic acids and amines, perhaps the most important reaction in the production of small-molecule pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals (Fig. 1b, Most used chemical transformations).29–32 From the insertive cross-coupling perspective, N-aryl benzamides have been synthesized from aryl halides, CO, and amines under transition metal catalysis (Fig. 1c, Strategies for amide synthesis).33–35 We wondered whether this logic could be extended to a doubly insertive (CO + NH) scheme involving SMC partners, among the most abundant organic building blocks in molecular discovery (Fig. 1c, Pd-catalyzed aminative carbonylation).

Our analysis indicates that the amide products accessible by this method are distinct from those of conventional amide coupling because of the divergent availability of aryl and vinyl fragments (Fig. 2). This distinction is significant because it shows that the current method is not simply an alternative route but instead provides access to a largely orthogonal region of amide chemical space (see Supporting Information, Section 2.6 for further discussion and analysis including comparison with aminocarbonylation method).

Below, we report a Pd-catalyzed aminative carbonylative cross-coupling that unifies Suzuki–Miyaura coupling and amide bond formation, enabling the convergent assembly of amide products from aryl/vinyl (pseudo)halides and aryl-/vinylboronic acids. The method can also be used to access some amides and enamides that are otherwise challenging to synthesize. The wide scope of the method allows for the repurposing of complex partners such as those found in pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals.36–40

## Results and Discussion

To begin reaction development, we examined a range of common supporting ligands, employing Pd(OAc)2 as a precatalyst and Mo(CO)6 as a CO surrogate due to its commercial availability and operational convenience. DBU was selected as the base, and O-(diphenylphosphinyl)hydroxylamine (DPPH, 2a) was employed as the nitrogen source.26,41,33 The use of Josiphos SL-J009–142 resulted in moderate reactivity towards desired product (16% yield) along with primary amide (9%) as the major byproduct, whereas catalysts modified with all other ligands were inactive (see Supporting Information, Section 2.3 for more details). As precatalysts, both Pd(dba)2 and Pd2(dba)3 were found to be inferior to Pd(OAc)2 (see Supporting Information, Section 2.3 for more details). Further examining precatalysts (Fig. 3, entries 1, 2, and 3),35,43 the Buchwald G3 precatalyst bearing SL-J009–1 proved best (91%, Fig. 3, entry 1). Inorganic bases, including KOH and K3PO4, were found to be less effective than DBU, while KOH gives rise to significant formation of primary amide (35%) (Fig. 3, entries 4 and 5; see Supporting Information, Section 2.3 for more details). While changes in reagent stoichiometry significantly affected product distribution, decreasing the equivalence of 2a and the organoboron coupling partner (3) resulted in diminished yields and increased the formation of the primary amide (Fig. 3, entries 6 and 7; see Supporting Information, Section 2.3 for more details), but increasing to 2.0 equivalents improved the outcome (Fig. 3, entry 1). Alternative CO surrogates, such as Fe(CO)5, were ineffective under these conditions (Fig. 3, entry 8). Reactions of electron-deficient arylboronic acids were difficult (Fig. 3, entry 9), potentially due to increased susceptibility to protodeboronation or competing decomposition pathways.44 A notable enhancement in reactivity was obtained by switching from boronic acids to boronate esters under otherwise identical conditions (Fig. 3, entry 10).45 A plausible mechanistic cycle (Fig. 4) was proposed in which base activation of the Pd G3 precatalyst generates the active Pd(0) species, which undergoes oxidative addition with the aryl halide to form complex I. Subsequent CO insertion affords the Pd–acyl intermediate II. Drawing on prior studies of aminative SMC reactions, Zhang proposed that 1,2-migration is energetically more favorable from a Pd-bound amido species than through a Pd-independent electrophilic amination pathway.26,27,46 Following ligand substitution to form complex III, coordination of the organoboron reagent in the presence of base promotes 1,2-migration to give intermediate V, and subsequent reductive elimination releases the amide product while regenerating Pd(0), thereby closing the catalytic cycle. An alternative pathway from III may also be plausible. Instead of engaging the aryl boronic acid, III could undergo 1,2-acyl migration to furnish IV′, followed by transmetalation and reductive elimination to deliver the amide product. Consistent with this possibility, omission of the aryl boronic acid leads to substantial formation of the primary amide 4a′ (see Supporting Information, Section 2.3, Table S7 for more details).

## Substrate scope

The scope of accessible products includes diverse N-aryl benzamides bearing a range of functional groups (Fig. 5). Aryl bromides and arylboron partners bearing electron-donating substituents (4a, 4b, 4d, 4e, 4f, 4g, 4h, 4i, 4j, 4k, 4l, 4m, 4n, 4o, 4p, 4q, 4r) and electron-withdrawing groups (4a, 4c, 4e, 4f, 4g, 4i, 4l, 4m, 4p) were successfully incorporated. Notably, aryl chlorides (4c, 4p) were retained in the amide products, providing the opportunity for subsequent cross-couplings. The benzocyclobutene moiety is tolerated (4h, 4av)47–49 as are multisubstituted and sterically encumbered bromides as in examples 4o and 4r.

The method accommodates heteroaromatic structures frequently found in drug-like molecules, including thiophenes, pyridines, pyrimidines, and pyridazines (4s, 4t, 4u, 4x, 4y, 4z, 4aa, 4ab, 4ac).50–52 Picolinamides, a structural class featured in some kinase inhibitors and agrochemicals,53,54 were converted in moderate yields (4s, 4z). Probenecid is used in the treatment of chronic gout,55 and derivatives were successfully synthesized under optimized conditions (4t and 4v). Amide derivatives (4u, 4x) of the antidiabetic drug canagliflozin were obtained in good yields.56 Pharmacophores such as cyclopropylamine (4aa) and azetidine (4ac) bearing pyrimidine motifs were also well tolerated under the reaction conditions.50,57 The tolerance of such pharmaceutically relevant functional groups highlights the practical utility of this four-component platform for rapid analogue generation.50 Aryl triflates are also suitable partners in this reaction including sterically encumbered examples (4ad, 4ae, 4af). Triflates derived from carvacrol afforded products 4ah and 4ai in good yields (Fig. 6).

The use of vinyl nucleophiles and electrophiles (instead of aryl) enables access to structurally complex and medicinally relevant scaffolds, including enamides, α,β-unsaturated amides, and α,β-unsaturated enamides (Fig. 6). Vinylboron partners are of particular significance as the corresponding enamines are unstable to hydrolysis and rarely commercially available.58–60 Our method provides a convenient route to functionalized enamides (4aj, 4ak, 4al, 4am, 4an, 4ao) from readily accessible aryl halides and vinyl boronic acids (pinacol esters).61 Product 4ak, bearing a valuable difluoroalkyl group, was obtained in 75% yield.62 Enaminones are a class of compounds with many members showing anticonvulsant activity.63,64 As an example, compound 4al was prepared in moderate yield. Vinylboronic acid pinacol esters bearing several common functional groups, such as ester (4an), acetal (4am), and trifluoromethyl (4ao) were successfully coupled to form enamides.

α,β-Unsaturated amides have attracted considerable attention in medicinal chemistry, most notably as electrophilic warheads in covalent inhibitors, and they are versatile intermediates in target-oriented synthesis as well.36,65,66 Convergent methods for the preparation of α,β-unsaturated amides (and especially enamides) are desirable.67–69 In our catalytic approach, vinyl triflates derived from norcamphor, (+)-camphor-, and the relatively strained (−)-verbenone were employed to synthesize α,β-unsaturated enamides 4ap, 4at, and 4ax. A pulegone-derived triflate was used to synthesize 4au in 33% yield without isomerization of the alkene. A series of α,β-unsaturated N-aryl amides (4aq, 4ar, 4as, 4au, 4av, 4aw, 4ay) were also obtained in moderate yields. However, aryl boronic acids that are both electron-rich and sterically congested remain challenging substrates under the current conditions. In addition, sterically congested aryl triflates are also less effective in this transformation (see Supporting Information, Section 2.7, for more details).

## Applications

Rapid diversity generation and exploration of structure-activity relationships (SAR) have become crucial to modern drug discovery.13,70 Methods that repurpose SMC partners can enable users to access analogs modularly and without extensive de novo synthesis.11,71 In one approach, Fenofibrate is synthesized through a series of classical transformations, including Friedel–Crafts acylation followed by demethylation and Williamson etherification.72 For the efficient synthesis of structural analogs, the use of Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling (SMC) partners provides a more modular strategy, enabling access to a broad range of core-modified analogs through systematic variation of coupling components (Fig. 7).20

The amide analog of fenofibrate can be obtained in excellent yield without compromising the aryl chloride (4az). Peripheral functionalization can still be easily achieved (4ba), simply by varying the aryl boronic acid coupling partner (Fig. 7). The amide analog was further derivatized using the latent chloride through other insertive coupling strategies. Nitrogen insertion between the amide (4az) and an aryl boronic acid (3t) can be achieved efficiently to give the elaborated product (4bb). In addition, by employing the same coupling partner (3t) while varying the inserted heteroatom, the corresponding complex diaryl ether derivative (4bc) can also be obtained. These examples illustrate how a toolbox of reactions repurposing SMC partners enables convenient assembly of diverse, medicinally relevant molecules in as few as two steps.

Though not directly related to the title transformation, an additional potential advantage of using Suzuki–Miyaura partners to construct amides lies in the ability to access “reversed” amide isomers from the same building blocks. The concept of amide reversal is a common strategic trope in drug design, as exemplified by the evolution of oncogenic kinase inhibitors following the groundbreaking development of imatinib, approved in 2001 (Fig. 8). In these systems, reversal of the amide bond can favorably alter the orientation of hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, by facilitating binding interactions within the kinase active site.40 This structural modification can also improve metabolic stability and modulate physicochemical properties. The generation of forward and reverse amide pairs often require diverging and sometimes lengthy sequences of functional group interconversions before amide coupling (Fig. 8). We reasoned that our insertive SMC strategy might allow for both isomers to be reached from a common set of coupling partners. Specifically, to formally reverse the inserted -C(O)NH- moiety, the aryl bromide would first be converted to the corresponding isocyanate via Pd catalysis73, followed by nucleophilic addition of the nucleophilic aryl to the aryl isocyanate through copper-catalyzed coupling (Fig. 8).74

As proof of principle, 4 aryl (pseudo)halides and 4 aryl boronate esters (X1–X4 and B1–B4) were selected to demonstrate the divergent synthesis of amide isomers (see Supporting Information, Section 3.3 for more details). Using slightly optimized conditions, X1 underwent efficient isocyanation followed by C–C coupling to yield the reverse amides (5a–5c) in moderate yields, corresponding to the normal amides 4a, 4f, and 4n. Carvacrol-derived triflate X2 was also engaged effectively under these conditions (5d, 5e, the complements of 4ah, 4ai). Using X3, an adapalene fragment, sequential isocyanation and amidation to furnish the desired amide (5f) in 26% yield over two steps, while normal coupling produced the corresponding normal isomer in 42% yield. This approach could provide access to isomeric pairs derived from probenecid: the aryl fragment of X4 (1h) was successfully incorporated at the N-terminus, affording 5g, or the C-terminus, affording 4v. Access to the amine analog of probenecid had previously entailed de novo synthesis involving reduction of a nitroarene precursor.

## Conclusion

In summary, we have developed a doubly insertive approach to access amides from SMC partners, both aryl and vinyl. The method employs low loadings of an accessible palladium precatalyst and abundant coupling partners with broad tolerance for variations in substrate electronic and steric properties. The potential synthetic applicability is highlighted by examples of bioactive heteroaromatic amides, enamides derived from natural terpenoids, relatively complex drug analogs, and the possibility of amide reversal. Variants of aminative cross-coupling with additional inserted components have the potential to generate other useful functional groups from repurposed building blocks. The development of such reactions and study of their mechanisms will be the focus of further research in our laboratory.
